title: Johor Data Centres' Rising Power Demand Forecast
abstract: A confidential forecast from Malaysia's grid operator suggests Johor's data centre corridor will strain the peninsula's power system sooner than publicly acknowledged.
body:
Malaysia's data centre boom in Johor is colliding with the limits of the peninsula's power system, according to a confidential forecast prepared by the national grid operator and reviewed by NotFinancialTimes. The document, dated 2026-04-18, projects that electricity demand from the Johor data centre corridor will reach 3.2 gigawatts by 2028, more than double the 1.4 gigawatts currently contracted. The forecast has not been made public and was circulated to a small group of officials at the Ministry of Energy and Water Transformation and the Energy Commission.

## The 3.2 GW projection and its implications

The 3.2 GW figure represents a 129 percent increase over contracted capacity. For context, Peninsular Malaysia's peak demand in 2025 was approximately 21 GW. The grid operator's forecast assumes that all announced data centre projects in Johor proceed on schedule, including campuses in Sedenak, Kulai, and Gelang Patah. If even half of the pipeline is built, the additional load would require the equivalent of two large combined-cycle gas turbines, neither of which is currently under construction.

A senior analyst at a Kuala Lumpur-based energy consultancy, who requested anonymity because the forecast is confidential, said the grid operator's internal modelling has become more conservative in recent months. "They are now stress-testing scenarios where demand arrives faster than generation and transmission upgrades," the analyst said. "The 3.2 GW number is not a worst case. It is a central case."

The Energy Commission declined to comment on the forecast. Tenaga Nasional Berhad, the national utility, did not respond to questions before publication.

## Why Johor's power system is vulnerable

Johor's electricity supply is currently balanced by a combination of local gas-fired generation and imports from the national grid. The state hosts several gas plants, but their output is already committed to existing industrial and residential demand. The new data centre load would be concentrated in a few districts, requiring significant upgrades to the 275 kV and 500 kV transmission network.

A 2025 study by the Energy Commission found that the southern region's transmission corridors have limited headroom for additional large loads. The study, which was not widely publicised, recommended that new data centre connections be phased in line with transmission reinforcements. Those reinforcements, including a new 500 kV line between Yong Peng and Sedenak, are not expected to be energised until 2029.

The grid operator's forecast notes that if data centre demand materialises before the transmission upgrades, the system could face localised constraints as early as 2027. In that scenario, the operator would need to curtail new connections or rely on emergency measures such as mobile generation units.

## The role of Singapore and regional competition

Johor's data centre growth is partly driven by spillover demand from Singapore, which has imposed a moratorium on new data centre construction since 2019. Operators seeking to serve the Singapore market have crossed the border, attracted by lower land and power costs. The Johor state government has approved more than 20 data centre projects since 2023, with a combined investment value of RM 45 billion.

However, the power constraint could slow that pipeline. A Singapore-based data centre developer, speaking on condition of anonymity, said his firm is now evaluating sites in Batam and Vietnam because of uncertainty over Johor's electricity supply. "We need firm capacity, not just a connection agreement," he said. "If the grid cannot guarantee 200 megawatts by 2027, we will go elsewhere."

The grid operator's forecast acknowledges this risk, noting that delays in power availability could push some projects to other countries. It estimates that up to 800 megawatts of planned capacity in Johor is at risk of relocation if transmission upgrades slip beyond 2028.

## What the forecast means for Malaysia's energy plans

The forecast has implications for Malaysia's broader energy transition. The government has targeted a 70 percent renewable energy share by 2050, but data centre demand is currently being met largely by gas-fired generation. The grid operator's document assumes that new gas plants will be needed to bridge the gap, even as Malaysia aims to reduce its carbon intensity.

A policy analyst at a regional think tank said the forecast exposes a tension between industrial policy and energy planning. "The data centre strategy was developed without a full accounting of the power system's limits," the analyst said. "Now the grid operator is essentially saying that the emperor has no clothes."

The Ministry of Energy and Water Transformation is expected to release a revised electricity supply plan later this year. Officials have signalled that the plan will include new gas plants and accelerated transmission projects, but no timeline has been announced.

For now, the 3.2 GW projection remains a confidential warning. If it proves accurate, Johor's data centre corridor will test the peninsula's power system in ways that have not been publicly anticipated. The grid operator's forecast concludes that without timely investment, the region could face a supply shortfall by 2028, forcing difficult choices between new connections and reliable service for existing customers.
